methods.label: Stirred
methods.blurb: Spirit only. Stir on ice until cold, strain, no dilution past that.

methods.label: Shaken
methods.blurb: Anything with juice, egg, or syrup carrying the drink. Hard shake, double strain.

cocktails.name: Pedro Martinez
cocktails.taste: Aged rum and sweet vermouth sit two to one, the Martinez ratio, with a quarter ounce of maraschino as the cherry glue. Ten dashes of Angostura is a bark flood, and three orange bitters keep peel in the mix. Two barspoons of absinthe is a pour you can taste, anise laid over the rum. Ice in the rocks glass is the point: this one is meant to sit and dilute.
cocktails.history: The Pedro Martinez is a rum Martinez from Michael Shea at Rum Club in Portland, Oregon, published by Imbibe in August 2020. Shea builds it on Demerara rum with Cocchi Vermouth di Torino, maraschino, aromatic bitters, orange bitters, and a few drops of absinthe, stirred and strained over a large cube. It is a modern sugarcane version of the gin Martinez, not a recipe from the nineteenth-century manuals. This card keeps the two-to-one rum and vermouth, the quarter of maraschino, and the rocks glass with ice, yet it pours ten dashes of Angostura and two barspoons of absinthe, heavier than Shea's drops.

cocktails.name: Rum Old Fashioned
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of aged rum, one barspoon of demerara, nothing more for sugar. The molasses of the syrup and the barrel of the rum are the same family, so the drink reads as rum first, then spice. Two dashes of Angostura and one of orange bitters keep clove and peel in the glass. Rocks, ice, and an orange twist: it sits.
cocktails.history: The Old-Fashioned takes its name from drinkers in the 1870s who asked for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail after bartenders began dressing the Whiskey Cocktail with absinthe, curacao, and other liqueurs. The formula itself is older: spirit, sugar, water, and bitters, the definition printed in The Balance and Columbian Repository in 1806. A rum Old-Fashioned is that template with the whiskey swapped out, a substitution that became common in craft bars in the 2000s as aged rum was treated as a sipping spirit. This card pours two ounces of aged rum, one barspoon of demerara syrup, two dashes of Angostura, and one of orange bitters, over ice with an orange twist.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, Old Fashioned cocktail history

cocktails.name: So So Cocktail
cocktails.taste: Equal gin and dry vermouth, a half ounce of apple brandy riding underneath, and a half ounce of grenadine that tastes of pomegranate. The gin is the drink; the apple is a peel of orchard. Dry vermouth keeps it lean, so the grenadine is the only roundness. Coupe, cherry.
cocktails.history: The So So Cocktail appears in Harry MacElhone's 1923 Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, credited to Mr. P. Soso, manager of Ciro's Club in London (MacElhone also names the Kit-Kat Club). The printed formula is one-sixth grenadine, one-sixth Calvados, one-third Cinzano vermouth, one-third gin. Harry Craddock repeats it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book with Italian vermouth in place of the brand. This card files under apple brandy and is mostly gin. It also swaps the Italian vermouth for dry, and it pours a half ounce of grenadine rather than a sixth.

cocktails.name: Dempsey
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces and a half of apple brandy and gin, so neither wins. Half an ounce of grenadine is a real pour, pomegranate against the orchard, and a quarter ounce of absinthe is enough anise to coat the glass. Stirred, no juice, coupe. Pink, wormwood-edged brandy and gin.
cocktails.history: Robert Vermeire prints the Dempsey in Cocktails How to Mix Them (1922) and says it was introduced at Deauville in 1921 after Jack Dempsey knocked out Georges Carpentier on 2 July 1921 at Boyle's Thirty Acres in Jersey City, the first million-dollar gate. Vermeire's formula is two-thirds Calvados to one-third gin, with dashes of absinthe and a teaspoon of grenadine. Harry MacElhone, the same year, credits Fred Martin at the Casino de Deauville in 1922, and uses a dash of Anis del Osa. Both claims stay in print. This card splits apple brandy and gin equally, then pours half an ounce of grenadine and a quarter ounce of absinthe, heavier than the dashes.

cocktails.name: Corpse Reviver No. 1
cocktails.taste: Cognac first, an ounce and a half, then three-quarters each of apple brandy and sweet vermouth. The apple is a second brandy. No juice, no bitters, stirred. Two brandies and vermouth, orchard under grape. Coupe, cherry.
cocktails.history: Harry Craddock prints Corpse Reviver No. 1 in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930: half brandy, a quarter apple brandy or Calvados, a quarter Italian vermouth, "to be taken before 11 a.m., or whenever steam and energy are needed." Difford's Guide notes that the drink is sometimes credited to Frank Meier at the Ritz Bar in Paris, although Meier makes no claim in his 1936 The Artistry of Mixing Drinks. The No. 2, gin, Lillet, orange liqueur, lemon, and absinthe, is a different cocktail and is not on this card. This one leads with cognac. The card pours an ounce and a half of cognac and three-quarters each of apple brandy and sweet vermouth.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, Corpse Reviver No.1 (Savoy recipe)

cocktails.name: Burnt Fuselage
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of cognac, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, so the orange is a third of the drink. Candied peel sits against the cognac; dry vermouth cuts the sugar. Stirred, no bitters, coupe, no twist. A stiff orange Manhattan, grape and peel.
cocktails.history: The Burnt Fuselage first appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, in the Cocktails Around Town section listing drinks of regulars at Harry's New York Bar in Paris. MacElhone credits Colonel C.W. Chuck Kerwood of Philadelphia, President of the International League of Aviators, who wanted a stiff steadier when he came down to earth: one-third Grand Marnier, one-third cognac, and one-third French vermouth. Kerwood was known as the wild man of aviation. This card keeps the equal parts and the coupe, with no bitters and no twist.

cocktails.name: Palace Hotel
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces and a half of cognac and sweet vermouth, grape on grape, a Manhattan ratio. One barspoon of orange liqueur is peel. No bitters. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. A brandy Manhattan with a thin orange film.
cocktails.history: A drink called Palace Hotel does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals under that name, nor in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The nearest parent is the Harvard, which George J. Kappeler prints in 1895 Modern American Drinks: equal brandy and Italian vermouth, gum, Angostura, and a seltzer top. Albert Stevens Crockett, in Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), ties the name to the college on the Charles. This card keeps the equal cognac and sweet vermouth and the lemon twist, yet it drops the bitters and the soda, and puts a barspoon of orange liqueur in their place.

cocktails.name: Metropole
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces and a half of cognac and dry vermouth, so neither wins. Two dashes of Peychaud's pull it toward cherry and anise. One dash of orange bitters is peel on the dry vermouth. Stirred, coupe, cherry. It reads pink and lean.
cocktails.history: George J. Kappeler prints the Metropole in 1895 Modern American Drinks as the house cocktail of the Hotel Metropole at Broadway and 42nd Street: equal brandy and French vermouth, gum, Peychaud's, orange bitters, and a cherry. It is a dry, Peychaud's turn on O.H. Byron's 1884 Metropolitan. Albert Stevens Crockett, in The Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), calls the hotel somewhat lively. The street-level Cafe Metropole held an all-night license; Herman Rosenthal was shot outside it in 1912, and the hotel went bankrupt that July. This card keeps Kappeler's equal parts, two dashes of Peychaud's, one of orange bitters, and the cherry. No gum.

cocktails.name: Brandy Crusta
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of cognac, then a quarter each of maraschino, demerara, and lemon. The lemon is an accent; the drink is still a cocktail. Two dashes of Angostura sit under cherry and brown sugar. Stirred. Rocks with ice and a lemon twist. It sits.
cocktails.history: Joseph Santini, an Italian bartender in New Orleans, built the Crusta in the 1850s, either at the City Exchange in the French Quarter or at Jewel of the South on Gravier Street, which he opened in 1855. Jerry Thomas prints it in the 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, misspelling Santini as Santina and calling him Spanish. The name is the sugar crust on the rim; the lemon is a dash, not a pour. David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, treats that citrus as an accent, and traces the Sidecar through the Daisy instead. This card pours two ounces of cognac, a quarter each of maraschino, demerara, and lemon, two dashes of Angostura, over ice, no crust.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Brandy Crusta

cocktails.name: Ritz
cocktails.taste: Three-quarters of an ounce of cognac, so this is a small drink. Half an ounce of maraschino is the sweet and the cherry; a quarter each of demerara and lemon. Three dashes of Angostura is a lot of bark for so little spirit. Stirred, coupe, flamed orange twist.
cocktails.history: Dale DeGroff built a Ritz Cocktail at Aurora in New York in 1985, later printed in The Craft of the Cocktail (2002) as a tribute to the Ritz drinks of Paris and Madrid: three-quarters cognac, half orange liqueur, a quarter each of maraschino and lemon, topped with Champagne, and a flamed orange twist. This card keeps the small cognac, the maraschino, the lemon, and the flamed twist. It drops the Champagne and the orange liqueur, adds a quarter of demerara and three dashes of Angostura, and stirs it.

cocktails.name: Old-Fashioned
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, one barspoon of demerara, two dashes of Angostura. The sugar is a film; the bitters are bark and clove against the corn. Rocks with ice. It sits.
cocktails.history: The cocktail itself is spirit, sugar, water, and bitters, defined in The Balance and Columbian Repository on 13 May 1806. By the 1870s bartenders were dressing the Whiskey Cocktail with curacao, maraschino, and absinthe; drinkers who wanted the older formula asked for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail. Robert Hess and David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, reject the Pendennis Club origin: Chicago papers were already talking about old-fashioned cocktails in 1880, a year before the Louisville club was founded. This card pours two ounces of bourbon, one barspoon of demerara, and two dashes of Angostura, over ice. No fruit.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Old-Fashioned Cocktail
Difford's Guide, Old Fashioned cocktail history

cocktails.name: Boulevardier
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of bourbon against a full ounce each of Campari and sweet vermouth. The whiskey leads a little; Campari is nearly a third of the drink. Stirred, rocks with ice. Bitter orange, grape, and corn whiskey, and the cube.
cocktails.history: The Boulevardier first appears in print in Harry MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, not in the main recipe list but in Arthur Moss's Cocktails Round Town essay, credited to Erskine Gwynne. Gwynne was an American in Paris who edited a monthly magazine of the same name from 1927 to 1932; Moss prints it as equal parts Campari, Italian vermouth, and bourbon. Ted Haigh notes that Americans had barely heard of Campari in 1927, and that the Negroni would not see print for another twenty years. This card keeps the bourbon and the rocks glass, yet it pours an ounce and a half of whiskey against an ounce each of Campari and sweet vermouth.

refs.title: Punch, In Search of the Ultimate Boulevardier

cocktails.name: Fancy Cocktail
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of bourbon, a quarter ounce of orange liqueur, one barspoon of demerara, two dashes of Angostura. The orange liqueur is peel and a little sugar. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. An Old-Fashioned with curacao in the sugar slot, served up.
cocktails.history: Jerry Thomas prints the Fancy Brandy Cocktail and Fancy Gin Cocktail in the 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide as the plain Cocktail strained into a fancy wine-glass, lemon on the rim and a piece of peel thrown on top. Wayne Curtis, in Imbibe, notes that the difference is mostly the glass. Thomas's later Improved Cocktail is the one that adds maraschino and absinthe; this card is the older fancy, whiskey with a splash of orange liqueur rather than those. This card pours an ounce and a half of bourbon, a quarter of orange liqueur, a barspoon of demerara, two dashes of Angostura, coupe, lemon.

cocktails.name: Manhattan
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon to one of sweet vermouth, so the whiskey leads. Two dashes of Angostura sit under the vermouth's grape and spice. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Corn, bark, and the cherry at the bottom.
cocktails.history: The Manhattan is American whiskey, Italian vermouth, and bitters, first named in print in an 1882 Gotham Gossip column syndicated out of New York, and first given a full recipe in O.H. Byron's 1884 The Modern Bartenders' Guide. The Manhattan Club dinner for Samuel Tilden in 1874, later tied to Jennie Jerome, is a late story: she was in England with a month-old Winston Churchill. William F. Mulhall, writing in 1923, credited a man named Black who kept a place on Broadway; David Wondrich found George Black's Manhattan Inn near Houston Street in the 1870s. Early books call for rye or bourbon, often at equal parts. This card files under bourbon, pours two to one, two dashes of Angostura, coupe, cherry.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Manhattan Cocktail

cocktails.name: Fancy Free
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, half an ounce of maraschino. One dash of Angostura, one of orange bitters. The cherry liqueur is almond and pit as much as fruit, and it does the sweetening. Stirred, rocks with ice, orange twist.
cocktails.history: The Fancy Free first appears in Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies' Companion, printed in 1941: a jigger of Fine Arts whiskey, two dashes of maraschino, a dash each of Angostura and orange bitters, shaken, strained into a sugar-rimmed cocktail glass. Gaige was a New York publisher and theatrical producer; Punch treats the naming as his. Revival bartenders, working from Milk & Honey spec sheets, dropped the sugar rim, stirred it, and poured it over ice with an orange twist. This card keeps the two ounces of bourbon, the half ounce of maraschino, one dash of each bitters, rocks, orange.

refs.title: Punch, Bring Back the Fancy Free

cocktails.name: Frisco
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, half an ounce of Bénédictine, nothing else. Honey, baking spice, and herbs against the whiskey. Stirred, rocks with ice. Short, sweet, herbal whiskey.
cocktails.history: The Frisco first prints in William "Cocktail Bill" Boothby's 1934 The World's Drinks and How to Mix Them as three-quarters of a jigger of whisky and a quarter of Bénédictine, stirred on a lump of ice with a lemon twist and a water chaser. Lucius Beebe repeats it in 1946 as two ounces of bourbon and three-quarters of Bénédictine, up. David Embury, in 1948, allows lemon juice; later books split the drink into a Frisco and a Frisco Sour. This card keeps Boothby's two-ingredient whiskey and Bénédictine, on bourbon, over ice, no juice and no twist.

cocktails.name: Derby
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon against three-quarters of an ounce of lime, so the lime is loud. Half an ounce each of sweet vermouth and orange liqueur dress it: grape and peel under the citrus. Stirred, despite the juice. Coupe, mint. Bourbon and lime sit in the same glass, cold.
cocktails.history: At least three drinks share the name Derby. The gin-and-peach-bitters version is Harry MacElhone, 1926, later in the Savoy. This card is the bourbon one: lime, sweet vermouth, and orange curacao, which Ted Haigh reprints from Trader Vic's 1947 Bartender's Guide, one of three Derbies Vic listed. Vic's formula is a short pour of bourbon against a heavy lime, and it is shaken. This card keeps the lime, the vermouth, the orange liqueur, and the mint, yet it pours two ounces of bourbon and stirs the drink.

cocktails.name: Cock 'n' Bull Special
cocktails.taste: Three-quarters of an ounce of bourbon, three-quarters of Bénédictine, so the herbal liqueur is a full partner. Half an ounce of cognac, a quarter of orange liqueur, one dash of Angostura. Stirred, rocks with ice. Honey, orange peel, grape, corn, and bark, a small drink that sits.
cocktails.history: The Cock 'n' Bull Special is named for Jack Morgan's British-style pub on Hollywood's Sunset Strip, opened in 1937 and later the house of the Moscow Mule. Ted Saucier prints it in Bottom's Up (1951) as a courtesy of the Cock 'n Bull: half an ounce of brandy, three-quarters each of Bénédictine and bourbon, a quarter of Cointreau, stirred, poured over a cube in a large chilled champagne glass, orange twist. The drink therefore dates between the bar's opening and 1951. This card keeps those measures and adds a dash of Angostura, over ice in a rocks glass, no twist.

cocktails.name: Rosita
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of tequila against a full ounce of Campari, so the bitter leads. Half an ounce each of sweet and dry vermouth split the wine, a Perfect Negroni with agave. One dash of Angostura is spice. Stirred, rocks, ice, orange twist.
cocktails.history: The Rosita first appears, creator unknown, in the 1974 Mr. Boston Official Bartender's Guide: one ounce tequila, one ounce Campari, half an ounce each of dry and sweet vermouth, stirred on cracked ice, lemon twist. Gary Regan reprinted it in The Bartender's Bible (1991) with more tequila and a dash of Angostura, then forgot he had. Terry Sullivan and Regan traced it back in 2007 in the San Francisco Chronicle. Mexico City is sometimes named; no period citation supports that. This card keeps Regan's ounce and a half of tequila and the dash of Angostura, yet it pours a full ounce of Campari and garnishes with orange.

cocktails.name: One Chance Fancy
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of tequila, a quarter of orange liqueur, a quarter of sweet vermouth. The vermouth is the sugar; the orange liqueur is peel. Two dashes of Angostura. Stirred, rocks, ice, orange twist. It drinks as a tequila Fancy Cocktail, spirit first, liqueur as dressing.
cocktails.history: Jerry Thomas prints the Fancy Brandy Cocktail in 1862 as the plain Cocktail strained into a wine glass with lemon on the rim: spirit, gum, bitters, and curacao. Brett Adams and Jacob Grier, in Raising the Bar (2022), still treat The Fancy as whiskey, orange liqueur, and bitters, an Old-Fashioned with a liqueur in the sugar slot. A drink called One Chance Fancy does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. This card puts the Fancy template on tequila, with a quarter ounce of sweet vermouth in the sugar slot, two dashes of Angostura, over ice with an orange twist.

refs.title: Willamette Week, Raising the Bar (The Fancy)

cocktails.name: Old Pal
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of rye, Campari, and dry vermouth, so Campari is a third of the drink. Bitter orange and rye heat sit against a dry wine cut, and one barspoon of demerara is brown sugar in a lean formula, rounding the Campari. Rocks with ice. It sits.
cocktails.history: The Old Pal first prints in Harry MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, not in the A-Z list but in Arthur Moss's Cocktails Round Town essay, the same appendix that carries the Boulevardier. Moss credits William "Sparrow" Robinson, sports editor of the New York Herald in Paris, with equal parts Canadian Club, Italian vermouth, and Campari, dedicated to Moss as My Old Pal. However, by the 1929 edition of Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails the vermouth is French, dry, and that is the formula that stuck. This card keeps equal rye, Campari, and dry vermouth, adds a barspoon of demerara, and pours it over ice.

refs.title: Serious Eats, The Old Pal and a New Friend

cocktails.name: Saratoga
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of rye, cognac, and sweet vermouth, so neither spirit leads. The cognac rounds the rye; two dashes of Angostura sit under grape and barrel. Stirred, coupe, lemon. A Manhattan that split the whiskey with brandy.
cocktails.history: David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, treats the Saratoga as two competing drinks that shared the name of the New York spa town. Jerry Thomas's posthumous 1887 Bar-Tenders Guide prints equal ponies of brandy, whiskey, and vermouth with two dashes of Angostura, shaken, in a claret glass with a quarter slice of lemon. Harry Johnson, the following year, printed a fancy brandy cocktail with a squirt of champagne. For thirty years the books took sides; by the 1930s both were a memory. This card is Thomas's split-base Manhattan: one ounce each of rye, cognac, and sweet vermouth, two dashes of Angostura, coupe, lemon.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Saratoga

cocktails.name: Monte Carlo
cocktails.taste: An ounce and three-quarters of rye against a half ounce of Benedictine. Honey, baking spice, and herbs ride on the whiskey, and one dash of Angostura is bark at the end. Rocks with ice. It sits.
cocktails.history: The Monte Carlo first prints in David Embury's 1948 The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks: one part Benedictine, two parts rye, one or two dashes of Angostura, shaken with cracked ice. Embury, a New York tax lawyer, called it a bit on the sweet side and suggested lemon juice and more rye. No bartender or bar is named. The drink is a Manhattan with Benedictine in place of vermouth, served here over ice. This card pours an ounce and three-quarters of rye, a half ounce of Benedictine, and one dash of Angostura.

cocktails.name: Improved Coctail
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of rye, then a barspoon each of maraschino, absinthe, and simple. The absinthe is in the drink, anise against cherry pit and sugar. Two dashes of Angostura. Rocks with ice, lemon. Rye first, then wormwood.
cocktails.history: Jerry Thomas prints the Improved Whiskey Cocktail in the 1876 Bar-Tender's Guide as the Improved Brandy Cocktail with whiskey in place of brandy: Boker's or Angostura, gum, maraschino, a dash of absinthe, lemon oil, shaken. The improvement is European liqueur on the old cocktail of spirit, sugar, and bitters, the same dressing drinkers later asked to skip when they called for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail. The card spells it Coctail, as the paper menu does. This card pours two ounces of rye, a barspoon each of maraschino, absinthe, and simple, two dashes of Angostura, over ice with a lemon twist.

refs.title: Eater, Building on a Classic: the Evolution of the Improved Cocktail

cocktails.name: Sazerac
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of rye, one barspoon of simple, four dashes of Peychaud's. The absinthe is a rinse, a thin anise film on the glass. Four dashes of Peychaud's is a lot: cherry and spice, enough to pink the drink. Rocks with no ice. The barspoon of sugar is the softness in it.
cocktails.history: The Sazerac takes its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, imported into New Orleans by Sewell Taylor around 1850 and poured at the Sazerac Coffee House with Antoine Peychaud's bitters. Thomas Handy took the bar around 1870; phylloxera wrecked French stocks, and rye replaced the cognac. Stanley Clisby Arthur's 1937 Famous New Orleans Drinks credits Leon Lamothe with the absinthe around 1870. However, David Wondrich treats the named drink as later, a bottled whiskey cocktail first printed by William T. Boothby in 1908. New Orleans named it the official cocktail of the city in 2008. This card pours two ounces of rye, one barspoon of simple, four dashes of Peychaud's, an absinthe rinse, rocks with no ice.

cocktails.name: Red Hook
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of rye, then a half ounce each of sweet vermouth and maraschino. The vermouth is grape and sugar; the cherry liqueur is almond and pit. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Rye first, then a thin cherry film.
cocktails.history: Vincenzo Errico built the Red Hook at Sasha Petraske's Milk & Honey in New York in 2003, a Manhattan crossed with a Brooklyn and named for the south Brooklyn neighborhood. Errico, an Italian bartender Petraske brought over after opening Milk & Honey London, used Punt e Mes, the bittersweet Turin vermouth, with rye and maraschino. He told Imbibe a fellow Italian neighbor in Brooklyn suggested the name. This card keeps the two ounces of rye and the half ounce of maraschino, yet it pours sweet vermouth in place of Punt e Mes.

cocktails.name: Waldorf
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of rye, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a quarter ounce of absinthe. The absinthe is in the drink, anise over grape, and two dashes of Angostura sit under both. Stirred, coupe, cherry. A Manhattan with wormwood in it.
cocktails.history: Jacques Straub prints the Waldorf in 1913 Manual of Mixed Drinks as equal rye, Italian vermouth, and absinthe, with two dashes of orange bitters, shaken. Albert Stevens Crockett repeats it in Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931) as a third each of whiskey, absinthe, and Italian vermouth, a dash of Manhattan bitters, frappe, from the old Waldorf Hotel on Fifth Avenue, demolished in 1929 for the Empire State Building. Dale DeGroff later cut the absinthe to a rinse. This card pours two ounces of rye, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a quarter ounce of absinthe, and two dashes of Angostura, coupe, cherry.

cocktails.name: The Slope
cocktails.taste: Two and a half ounces of rye, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a quarter of apricot liqueur. Stone fruit against a large rye pour. One dash of Angostura. Stirred, coupe, cherry. The apricot is orchard on a Manhattan.
cocktails.history: Julie Reiner built The Slope in 2006 and named it for Park Slope, first served at Flatiron Lounge, then as the house Manhattan at Clover Club, which she opened in Brooklyn in 2008. Jim Meehan printed the rye, Punt e Mes, apricot, and Angostura formula in GQ in 2010. This card keeps the two and a half ounces of rye, three-quarters vermouth, and a quarter of apricot, yet it pours sweet vermouth in place of Punt e Mes.

refs.title: GQ, The Platinum Age of the Cocktail

cocktails.name: Vieux Carré
cocktails.taste: Three-quarters of an ounce each of rye, cognac, and sweet vermouth, equal and small. One barspoon of Benedictine is honey and herbs. One dash of Angostura, one of Peychaud's. Rocks with ice, lemon. Split-base Manhattan with an herbal film.
cocktails.history: Walter Bergeron, head bartender at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans, built the Vieux Carré in the 1930s and named it for the French Quarter, the old square. Stanley Clisby Arthur prints it in 1937: equal rye, cognac, and Italian vermouth, a half teaspoon of Benedictine, a dash each of Peychaud's and Angostura. The Carousel Bar, where the drink now lives, opened in 1949; Bergeron was mixing it in the hotel's earlier lounge. Chuck Taggart, in The Oxford Companion, notes Bergeron had worked the bar before Prohibition and returned at Repeal. This card keeps the equal three-quarters and both bitters, with a barspoon of Benedictine, over ice with a lemon twist.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Vieux Carré

cocktails.name: Cocktail de la Louisiane
cocktails.taste: Equal three-quarters of rye, sweet vermouth, and Benedictine, so the herbal liqueur is a third of the drink. Two barspoons of absinthe is anise you can taste. Three dashes of Peychaud's. Stirred, coupe, lemon and cherry. Honey, wormwood, and rye.
cocktails.history: Stanley Clisby Arthur prints Cocktail à la Louisiane in Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em (1937) as the special cocktail of Restaurant de la Louisiane, a French Quarter Creole house opened in 1881: equal rye, Italian vermouth, and Benedictine, three or four dashes each of absinthe substitute and Peychaud's, strained onto a cherry. Whether it predates Walter Bergeron's Vieux Carré is disputed; both first see print in Arthur's book. This card keeps Arthur's equal three-quarters, pours two barspoons of absinthe and three dashes of Peychaud's, coupe, lemon and cherry.

refs.title: Saveur, Drink the Secret Cocktail of New Orleans

cocktails.name: Bobby Burns
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of scotch against a full ounce of sweet vermouth, so the grape sits nearly even with the malt. Half an ounce of Bénédictine is honey and herbs, a pour not a dash, enough to coat the drink. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Scotch first, then the liqueur's spice.
cocktails.history: The Bobby Burns is a Scotch Manhattan with Bénédictine. Harry Craddock prints it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 as equal Italian vermouth and Scotch whisky with three dashes of Bénédictine. Albert Stevens Crockett, a year later in Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Days, lists a Robert Burns with absinthe and orange bitters, and says it may have been named for the poet or for a cigar salesman who bought at the old Waldorf bar. Earlier printings use Baby Burns (Bishop and Babcock, 1900) and Robert Burns (Grohusko, 1910). This card keeps Craddock's scotch, sweet vermouth, and Bénédictine, yet it pours an ounce and a half of whiskey, a full ounce of vermouth, and a half ounce of the liqueur.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, Bobby Burns cocktail history
The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Bobby Burns

cocktails.name: Affinity
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of scotch, then three-quarters each of sweet and dry vermouth, so the whiskey leads and the vermouths split. Two dashes of Angostura sit under both. Stirred, coupe, lemon and cherry. A Perfect Manhattan on scotch: malt, grape, and bark.
cocktails.history: The Affinity first appears in The New York Sun on 28 October 1907 as a Broadway cocktail of Scotch whisky, Italian vermouth, powdered sugar, and orange bitters. The version that stuck, equal French vermouth, Italian vermouth, and Scotch with aromatic bitters, prints in Jacob A. Didier's The Reminder in 1909, is repeated by Hugo Ensslin in 1917, and is the formula Harry Craddock puts in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930. This card keeps both vermouths and two dashes of Angostura, yet it pours an ounce and a half of scotch against three-quarters of each vermouth, so the whiskey leads.

refs.title: The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Affinity Cocktail

cocktails.name: Rob Roy
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of scotch to one of sweet vermouth, the Manhattan ratio. Two dashes of orange bitters, not Angostura, so peel rather than bark sits under the malt. Stirred, coupe, no garnish on the card. Leaner than a bourbon Manhattan, orange oil in the grape.
cocktails.history: The Rob Roy is a Scotch Manhattan, named for Reginald De Koven and Harry B. Smith's 1894 Broadway operetta about the Highland outlaw Robert Roy MacGregor. The Waldorf-Astoria, then on Fifth Avenue near Herald Square Theatre, is the usual credit; other writers point to the Fifth Avenue Hotel. David Wondrich found Henry A. Orphal at Duke's House in Hoboken, around 1895, swapping Scotch into a Manhattan for a whisky salesman who would not drink anything else. Early books often use orange bitters; later ones shift to Angostura. This card keeps two ounces of scotch, one of sweet vermouth, and two dashes of orange bitters, coupe.

cocktails.name: Scotch Old-Fashioned
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of scotch, one barspoon of simple, one dash of Angostura and one of orange bitters. The sugar is a film; peel and bark sit under the malt. Stirred, rocks with ice. Scotch first, then the two bitters against the whiskey.
cocktails.history: The cocktail is spirit, sugar, water, and bitters, defined in The Balance and Columbian Repository on 13 May 1806. By the 1870s bartenders were dressing the Whiskey Cocktail with curacao and absinthe; drinkers who wanted the older formula asked for an old-fashioned whiskey cocktail. Scotch is one of the spirits that definition already allowed. This card pours two ounces of scotch, one barspoon of simple, one dash of Angostura and one of orange bitters, over ice. No fruit.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Old-Fashioned Cocktail
Difford's Guide, Old Fashioned cocktail history

cocktails.name: Automobile
cocktails.taste: Three-quarters of an ounce each of scotch, gin, and sweet vermouth, so none of the three wins. Two dashes of orange bitters keep peel in the mix. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Juniper against malt, grape in the middle. A short equal-parts drink: two and a quarter ounces before the ice.
cocktails.history: Jacques Straub prints an Auto Cocktail in 1914 Drinks as equal French vermouth, Tom gin, and Scotch whiskey, shaken. Frank Meier, at the Ritz Bar in Paris, prints the Automobile in The Artistry of Mixing Drinks in 1934: a dash of orange bitters and one-third each of Italian vermouth, gin, and Scotch whisky, stirred. This card follows Meier. It pours three-quarters of an ounce each of scotch, gin, and sweet vermouth, two dashes of orange bitters, coupe, cherry.

cocktails.name: Country Club
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of light rum against a full ounce of dry vermouth, nearly even. Half an ounce of orange liqueur is peel and sugar, and one dash of orange bitters sits under both. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Lean rum, dry grape, candied orange.
cocktails.history: Albert Stevens Crockett prints the Country Club in the 1935 Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book as half Bacardi, half French vermouth, and a dash of orange curaçao, among the amendments to the old Waldorf list. William T. Boothby's 1934 World Drinks has a different Country Club, whiskey with orange bitters in a bar glass. The Savoy Country Club Cooler is French vermouth, grenadine, and soda, a different drink. This card keeps Crockett's light rum, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, yet it pours an ounce and a half of rum, a full ounce of vermouth, a half ounce of orange liqueur, and a dash of orange bitters, coupe, lemon.

cocktails.name: Yacht Club
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of light rum to one of sweet vermouth, a Manhattan ratio on cane. A quarter ounce of apricot liqueur is stone fruit, not a dash. Stirred, coupe, no twist on the card. Rum first, then grape, then a thin apricot film.
cocktails.history: A Yacht Club Cocktail of rum, Italian vermouth, and apricot prints in the 1948 Ron Daiquiri Coctelera booklet from Havana: two-thirds Daiquiri rum, one-third Italian vermouth, a dash of apricot brandy, stirred. David Embury includes a Yacht Club of the same bones in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks the same year; Difford's adapts that printing. This card keeps the two-to-one rum and sweet vermouth and puts a quarter ounce of apricot liqueur in place of the dash.

refs.title: 1948 Ron Daiquiri Coctelera, Yacht Club Cocktail

cocktails.name: Tipsy Coachman
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of vodka, three-quarters of Bénédictine, one dash of Angostura. Honey and herbs, vodka as the thinner so the liqueur is a third of the drink. Stirred, rocks with ice, lemon twist. It sits, herbal and sweet, with bark at the end.
cocktails.history: The formula is the Gypsy Queen: vodka, Bénédictine, and bitters. David Wondrich found the earliest printing in a 1938 booklet from New York's Russian Tea Room, one of the first American vodka cocktails. David Embury reprints it in 1948 as Gypsy or Gypsy Queen and prefers a drier ratio than the original one-to-two. A drink called Tipsy Coachman does not appear under that name in those books; the phrase is older, from Oliver Goldsmith, and later a legal doctrine. This card keeps the ounce and a half of vodka, three-quarters of Bénédictine, and a dash of Angostura, over ice with a lemon twist.

cocktails.name: Vodka Martini
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of vodka, half an ounce of dry vermouth. Four to one; the wine is in the drink. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Cold, grape.
cocktails.history: A vodka Martini prints in a 1935 Smirnoff pamphlet at three parts vodka to one of French vermouth, with lemon peel in the mixing glass. Lucius Beebe puts two versions in The Stork Club Bar Book in 1946. Ted Saucier, in 1952 Bottoms Up, credits photographer Jerome Zerbe with a four-to-one Vodkatini and a lemon twist. John G. Martin at Heublein spent the 1940s and 1950s selling Smirnoff as a mixer. This card is two ounces of vodka to half an ounce of dry vermouth, stirred, coupe, lemon.

cocktails.name: Quill
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth, so Campari is a third of the drink, then a quarter ounce of absinthe in the mix, not a rinse. That is a real pour of anise, enough to sit on the Campari rather than perfume the glass. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. Bitter orange, grape, and wormwood, served up.
cocktails.history: The Quill first prints in the 1996 edition of Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, where Andrew and Duncan MacElhone added forty-odd recipes to Harry MacElhone's original books and credited this one to Frank C. Payne of New York. It is not in the earlier editions, nor in MacElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails. Payne was a theatrical press agent in the Theatrical Press Representatives of America, which published a magazine called The Quill. The drink is a Negroni with absinthe. This card keeps the equal ounces and puts a quarter ounce of absinthe in the build, coupe, orange twist.

refs.title: Serious Eats, If You Like Negronis, Try the Quill

cocktails.name: Negroni
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth. Campari is a third of the drink: bitter orange against grape and juniper. Stirred, rocks with ice, no twist on the card. The cube is the dilution, so the Campari stays loud as it sits.
cocktails.history: The usual story puts Count Camillo Negroni at Caffe Casoni on Via de' Tornabuoni in Florence around 1919, asking Fosco Scarselli to stiffen his Americano with gin in place of soda. Luca Picchi reconstructed that account in 2002; it is the better-supported one. However, Colonel Hector Andres Negroni later said there was no Camillo in the family tree and pointed instead to General Pascal Olivier Comte de Negroni. The equal-parts formula does not see print until Amedeo Gandiglio's 1947 Cocktails Portfolio. This card pours one ounce each of gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth, over ice, no garnish letter.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, History of the Negroni
Punch, The Negroni Has a Secret

cocktails.name: Claridge
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of gin and dry vermouth, then a half ounce each of apricot liqueur and orange liqueur, so the two liqueurs together match the gin. Stone fruit and candied peel sit against a dry wine cut. Stirred, coupe, no twist on the card. Apricot and orange on a wet Martini.
cocktails.history: Harry MacElhone prints the Claridge in 1922 Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, credited to Leon, bartender at Claridge's Hotel on the Champs-Elysees in Paris: one-third gin, one-third French vermouth, one-sixth apricot brandy, one-sixth Cointreau. Harry Craddock repeats the formula in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, and prints the same measures again as the Frankenjack. The London hotel of the same name is a later guess; Leon's Paris house is the one in the book. This card keeps equal gin and dry vermouth and a half ounce of each liqueur, stirred, coupe.

refs.title: The 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, Claridge Cocktail

cocktails.name: Lucien Gaudin
cocktails.taste: An ounce of gin against half ounces of Campari, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, so gin leads and the three modifiers split. Bitter orange and candied peel sit against a dry wine cut, leaner than a Negroni and more orange. Stirred, coupe, orange twist.
cocktails.history: Named for Lucien Gaudin, a French fencer who won gold in foil and epee at the 1924 Paris Olympics and again in 1928 at Amsterdam. The drink first prints in RIP's 1929 Cocktails de Paris, credited to Charlie of Le Cheval Pie, a Paris restaurant that ran from 1925 to 1930, and it took the Coupe d'honneur at the Professional Bartenders Championship in Paris on 2 February 1929. RIP is Georges Gabriel Thenon. This card pours an ounce of gin and a half ounce each of Campari, dry vermouth, and orange liqueur, coupe, orange.

refs.title: Cold Glass, The Lucien Gaudin Cocktail

cocktails.name: Martinez
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin against a full ounce of sweet vermouth and a half of dry, so the wine is wet and split. A quarter ounce of maraschino is cherry pit and almond, and one dash each of orange bitters and Angostura keep peel and bark in the mix. Stirred, coupe, orange. It drinks as a gin Manhattan with both vermouths and a cherry film.
cocktails.history: O.H. Byron prints the Martinez in 1884 The Modern Bartender's Guide as "Same as Manhattan, only you substitute gin for whisky," on a page with two Manhattan formulas. Jerry Thomas's posthumous 1887 Bar-Tender's Guide gives the first full spec: a pony of Old Tom gin, a wine-glass of vermouth, two dashes of maraschino, a dash of Boker's bitters. The California stories, Jerry Thomas at the Occidental and Julio Richelieu in Martinez, stay unproven. This card pours an ounce and a half of gin, both vermouths, a quarter of maraschino, and one dash each of orange bitters and Angostura, coupe, orange.

cocktails.name: Ford Cocktail
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces and a half of gin and dry vermouth, then a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, honey and herbs as a pour rather than a dash. Two dashes of orange bitters keep peel in the mix. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. A wet Martini with an herbal film.
cocktails.history: George J. Kappeler prints the Ford Cocktail in 1895 Modern American Drinks: three dashes of Bénédictine, three dashes of orange bitters, half a jigger of Tom gin, half a jigger of French vermouth, orange peel. He does not name a Ford. Ted Haigh, in Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, points to Malcolm Webster Ford, the 1880s all-around athlete and journalist, rather than Henry, whose company postdates the recipe. This card keeps the equal gin and dry vermouth and the orange bitters, yet it pours a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, coupe, orange.

cocktails.name: Journalist
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin, then a half ounce each of sweet and dry vermouth, a Perfect Martini ratio. A quarter ounce of orange liqueur and a quarter ounce of lemon sit in the same glass: peel and pith, enough lemon that the drink is tart even stirred. One dash of Angostura. Coupe, lemon twist. Citrus in a stirred gin drink.
cocktails.history: Harry Craddock prints the Journalist in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930: two-thirds Gordon's dry gin, one-sixth each of French and Italian vermouth, two dashes of lemon juice, two dashes of curaçao, one dash of Angostura, shaken. No bartender is named. Paul Clarke, in Serious Eats, treats it as a Perfect Martini with dashes of lemon and orange liqueur. This card keeps both vermouths and the Angostura, yet it pours a quarter ounce each of orange liqueur and lemon, stirred, coupe, lemon.

refs.title: The 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, Journalist Cocktail

cocktails.name: Vancouver
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of dry vermouth, so the wine is a real pour, then a half ounce of Bénédictine, honey and herbs nearly even with the vermouth. One dash of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. Gin first, then the liqueur's spice on a dry wine.
cocktails.history: The Vancouver prints in the About Town Cocktail Book, issued in Vancouver around 1925 by Mitchell Publishing: fifty percent gin, thirty percent French vermouth, twenty percent Bénédictine, a dash of orange bitters, olive. Joseph A. Fitchett, head bar steward of the Vancouver Club, checked the recipes. A later story, told to Steve da Cruz in 2006, put a sweet-vermouth version at the Sylvia Hotel after 1954. Alex Black, in Scout Magazine in 2020, showed that the 1925 Vancouver used dry vermouth; the sweet one in the same book is the Fitchett. This card keeps dry vermouth: an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters vermouth, a half ounce of Bénédictine, and one dash of orange bitters, coupe, orange.

refs.title: Scout Magazine, We've Been Making the Vancouver Cocktail Wrong

cocktails.name: Wiffin
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of sweet vermouth, then a half ounce of cognac, grape spirit under gin. One dash of absinthe is a thin anise wash, not a pour. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Two spirits and vermouth, wormwood at the edge.
cocktails.history: The Wiffin is not a pre-1970 bar-book drink. P. G. Wodehouse, in the 1928 story "The Passing of Ambrose," has Ambrose Wiffin sketch a cocktail of gin, Italian vermouth, a spot of old brandy, and a dash of absinthe. David Wondrich reconstructed the formula in Australian Bartender in 2011: English gin, Italian vermouth, cognac, and a dash or two of absinthe. This card pours an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters sweet vermouth, a half ounce of cognac, and one dash of absinthe, coupe, lemon.

refs.title: David Wondrich, The Wiffin, Australian Bartender

cocktails.name: Fitchett
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of sweet vermouth, then a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, honey and herbs as a film rather than a half-ounce pour. One dash of orange bitters. Stirred, coupe, cherry. Gin first, grape, then a thin herbal coat. Wetter and less herbal than the Vancouver on this card.
cocktails.history: The Fitchett prints in the same About Town Cocktail Book as the Vancouver, around 1925. The unnamed writer credits Joseph A. Fitchett, head bar steward of the Vancouver Club: of the thousand and one drinks he can mix, it is the best. The formula is fifty percent gin, thirty percent Italian vermouth, twenty percent Bénédictine, a dash of orange bitters, olive or cherry. It is the sweet-vermouth sibling of the Vancouver in that book. This card keeps the gin and sweet vermouth, yet it pours only a quarter ounce of Bénédictine, coupe, cherry.

refs.title: Scout Magazine, We've Been Making the Vancouver Cocktail Wrong

cocktails.name: Martini
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin to one of dry vermouth, so the wine is a third of the drink, not a rinse. One dash of orange bitters is peel in the glass. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. It drinks wet and cold: juniper, then the vermouth's wormwood and grape, then a thin orange film.
cocktails.history: The first gin-and-vermouth drinks print in 1883 newspaper copy from Cleveland and Chicago, still called Manhattans, then as Martinez in O.H. Byron's 1884 The Modern Bartender's Guide and as Martini in Harry Johnson's 1888 Bartenders' Manual: Old Tom, sweet vermouth, curaçao, gum, and bitters. The Dry Martini, French vermouth and a drier gin, is named in New York by 1896 and is the dominant version by 1900. Two-to-one gin to vermouth appears in the late 1890s and is standard by the 1910s; orange bitters stay until the 1940s, then drop as the ratio marches past five-to-one. This card keeps the wet 2:1, one dash of orange bitters, coupe, lemon.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Martini

cocktails.name: Villa Straylight
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin to one of dry vermouth, the wet Martini on this card, then a half ounce of orange liqueur as candied peel, and a barspoon of absinthe in the mix, not a rinse. The anise is a pour you can taste, laid over the orange. Stirred, coupe, no garnish. Wet gin, peel, and wormwood.
cocktails.history: Villa Straylight does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. It is a house drink on this card, named for the Tessier-Ashpool villa at the end of Freeside in William Gibson's 1984 Neuromancer. The build is this card's wet Martini, two ounces of gin to one of dry vermouth, plus a half ounce of orange liqueur and a barspoon of absinthe in the mix. Harry Johnson's 1888 Martini already carried orange curaçao; the absinthe is the Tuxedo's anise, poured rather than rinsed. Coupe, no garnish.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, Tuxedo cocktail and its many variations

cocktails.name: Casino
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin, a half ounce of maraschino, two dashes of orange bitters. The cherry liqueur is almond and pit as much as fruit, and it does the sweetening; there is no lemon. Stirred. Rocks with ice and a cherry. It sits: gin first, then a cherry film, and the cube.
cocktails.history: Jacob A. Didier prints the Casino in 1909 The Reminder: two dashes each of maraschino, orange bitters, and lemon juice, a drink of Tom gin, stirred, cherry. Hugo R. Ensslin copies it almost verbatim in 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks, and Harry Craddock repeats it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book. David Embury, in 1948, swaps orange juice for the bitters and tells you to mix it like an Aviation. This card drops the lemon, pours a half ounce of maraschino rather than dashes, keeps two dashes of orange bitters, and serves it over ice in a rocks glass with a cherry.

refs.title: The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Casino Cocktail

cocktails.name: Dry Orange Martini
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin, three-quarters of dry vermouth, a quarter ounce of orange liqueur, two dashes of orange bitters. The vermouth still leads the dressing; the liqueur is peel and a little sugar, not a third of the drink. Stirred, coupe. Drier than this card's Martini, with candied orange instead of a twist.
cocktails.history: Wayne Collins built the Dry Orange Martini in 2003 for Maxxium UK: two ounces of gin, three-quarters of dry vermouth, a quarter of orange liqueur, two dashes of orange bitters. Collins was a London bartender who ran Mixxit, Maxxium's training programme, and later put the White Negroni into wider print. The parent is the Dry Martini; Harry Johnson's 1888 Martini already carried orange curaçao, which later books dropped as the drink dried out. This card keeps Collins's measures and the coupe.

cocktails.name: Tuxedo #2
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin against three-quarters of dry vermouth, so the gin leads. A quarter ounce of maraschino is cherry pit and almond, and three dashes of orange bitters is a lot of peel. The absinthe is a rinse, a thin anise film on the glass rather than a pour. Stirred, coupe, orange twist. A dressed Martini, gin first, then cherry, peel, and wormwood.
cocktails.history: Harry Johnson prints the Tuxedo in his 1900 Bartenders' Manual: equal Old Tom and French vermouth, dashes of maraschino, absinthe, and orange bitters. The name is the Tuxedo Club in Tuxedo Park, New York, opened in 1886. Harry Craddock, in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, splits the family: his No. 1 is gin, dry vermouth, lemon peel, and absinthe; his No. 2 is Johnson's original with dry gin in place of Old Tom. This card's Tuxedo #2 keeps the maraschino, the orange bitters, and the absinthe, yet it pours two ounces of gin to three-quarters of vermouth, a quarter of maraschino, three dashes of bitters, and an absinthe rinse, coupe, orange.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, Tuxedo cocktail and its many variations
The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Tuxedo Cocktail (No. 2)

cocktails.name: Duplex
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces and a half of sweet and dry vermouth, so neither wins. Two dashes of orange bitters are peel on the split wine. Stirred, no spirit, coupe, orange twist. Grape and spice, cold, with a thin orange film on the wine.
cocktails.history: Albert Stevens Crockett, in Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), lists the Duplex as equal Italian and French vermouth with two dashes of orange bitters or two squeezes of orange peel, and calls it parent of the original Bronx. Johnnie Solon of the Waldorf said he was making a Duplex when Traverson, head waiter of the Empire Room, challenged him to invent a new cocktail, and he added gin and orange juice. This card is the Waldorf Duplex: an ounce and a half of each vermouth, two dashes of orange bitters, stirred, coupe, orange twist.

refs.title: Albert Stevens Crockett, Old Waldorf Bar Days (1931), Duplex
Crockett, Old Waldorf Bar Days, Solon on the Bronx

cocktails.name: Vermouth Panaché
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of sweet vermouth to one of dry, so the sweet leads. One dash of orange bitters is peel on the grape. Stirred, coupe, lemon twist. Grape and spice, the sweet vermouth leading, with a thin lemon oil on top.
cocktails.history: Panache is French for mixed. Philip Greene, in To Have and Have Another (2012), gives the name Vermouth Panache to a drink Ernest Hemingway described in a 1934 Esquire piece: on a fishing trip off Havana, French and Italian vermouth over ice with a dash of bitters and a lemon peel. Hemingway did not name it. Greene's reconstruction, as printed in Saveur, is three ounces dry to one sweet, Angostura, on the rocks. This card inverts the ratio, two sweet to one dry, uses orange bitters, and pours it up with a lemon twist.

cocktails.name: Winter Daiquiri
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of aged rum against a full ounce of lime and only a half ounce of demerara: tart, brown sugar, barrel. Two dashes of Angostura pull clove and bark through the lime. Coupe.
cocktails.history: The Daiquiri is credited to Jennings Stockton Cox, an American mining engineer at Daiquiri, Cuba, around the turn of the twentieth century, mixing Bacardi, lime, and sugar. Francesco Domenico Pagliuchi wrote in 1948 that he was there and suggested the name; Basil Woon's 1928 When It's Cocktail Time in Cuba records Cox naming it at Santiago's Venus bar. The first recipe-book appearance is Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks, misspelt Daiguiri. A winter version keeps the sour and changes the rum and the sugar. This card uses aged rum, demerara syrup, a full ounce of lime against a half ounce of sweetener, and two dashes of Angostura.

cocktails.name: Air Mail
cocktails.taste: A rum sour of an ounce and a half of aged rum, three-quarters lime, three-quarters honey, then two ounces of Champagne over ice in a rocks glass. Honey is thicker and waxier than sugar, so the rum tastes darker than a Daiquiri. The bubbles and the melt are the lift.
cocktails.history: The Air Mail first saw print in Bacardi and Its Many Uses, a 1930 pamphlet from the still-Cuban company. Jeff Berry, writing in The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, notes that Cuba began air-mail service that year, yet the pamphlet names no bartender. W.C. Whitfield's 1941 Here's How prints it as rum, lime, honey, and Champagne in a highball, with the line "It ought to make you fly high." Some later writers treat it as a rum French 75. The early printings, however, are a honey Daiquiri topped with sparkling wine and served long, over ice. This card keeps the honey and the Champagne, uses aged rum, and pours it in a rocks glass with ice.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, Air Mail

cocktails.name: Brass Rail
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of aged rum, a half of Benedictine, a full ounce of lemon, a half of simple: a rum sour with a herbal liqueur in the sugar slot. Egg white gives it a foam cap. Two dashes of orange bitters sit in the shake; three dashes of Angostura are dropped on the foam, clove and bark on the white. Coupe.
cocktails.history: Tony Abou-Ganim built the Brass Rail as a nightcap for his cousin Helen David, who favored Benedictine, and named it for her bar in Port Huron, Michigan, which she opened in 1937. Difford's Guide adapts the recipe from Abou-Ganim: aged rum, Benedictine, lemon, sugar, egg white, and orange bitters, with a flamed orange twist and cinnamon on the foam. This card uses aged rum, Benedictine, a full ounce of lemon, half an ounce of simple, two dashes of orange bitters, egg white, and three dashes of Angostura dropped on the foam.

cocktails.name: Jack Rose
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of apple brandy, three-quarters lime, three-quarters grenadine. Lime, so the sour is sharp and green. Equal grenadine means the drink is as pink as it is tart; the apple sits under pomegranate. Shaken. Coupe.
cocktails.history: David Wondrich traces the Jack Rose to Frank Haas at Fred Eberlin's downtown New York bar, named in the New York Press in 1899. Jacob Grohusko's 1908 Jack's Manual is the first printed formula. By Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks it had become applejack, lime, and grenadine. The name is disputed: Wondrich favors the General Jacqueminot, or Jack, rose, a pink hybrid the drink resembles; Frank J. May claimed it in the 1905 Police Gazette; Bald Jack Rose, the 1912 Rosenthal-case informant, is a later story, and the drink predates him. This card is Straub's three-ingredient drink: an ounce and a half of apple brandy, three-quarters lime, three-quarters grenadine.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Jack Rose

cocktails.name: Pink Lady
cocktails.taste: Gin at an ounce and a half, then three-quarters of apple brandy and three-quarters of lime, a half ounce of grenadine, and egg white. The foam is the texture; the apple is a real pour. Lime and gin keep it sharp. Grenadine is color and a little pomegranate. Coupe, cherry.
cocktails.history: The Pink Lady takes its name from Ivan Caryll's 1911 Broadway musical, starring Hazel Dawn. Wondrich records that the drink mixed for her at Murray's Roman Gardens was ojen with Peychaud's and Angostura, not this one. Jacques Straub's 1913 Manual of Mixed Drinks prints the version that entered the books: equal gin, applejack, and lime, with dashes of grenadine, and no egg. Later recipes drop the apple brandy, add egg white or cream, or both. Craddock's Savoy omits the applejack and adds the white. This card keeps Straub's gin, apple brandy, lime, and grenadine, and it shakes egg white with them.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, Pink Lady Cocktail

cocktails.name: Honeymoon
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a quarter of apple brandy against a full ounce of Benedictine: herb almost even with orchard. A barspoon of orange liqueur and a dash of orange bitters are peel. Half an ounce of lemon lifts it. Rocks, ice, orange twist: it sits and the Benedictine warms.
cocktails.history: Hugo R. Ensslin first prints the Honey Moon Cocktail in Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1916): equal Benedictine and apple brandy, juice of half a lemon, three dashes of curacao. Ensslin was at the Hotel Wallick in Times Square. Craddock copies it into the Savoy in 1930. It later turns up at the Brown Derby in Los Angeles, and David Embury (1948) also calls it the Farmer's Daughter, with a much drier applejack-forward ratio. This card pours an ounce and a quarter of apple brandy, a full ounce of Benedictine, a barspoon of orange liqueur, half an ounce of lemon, and a dash of orange bitters, over ice with an orange twist.

cocktails.name: Southern Point
cocktails.taste: Four equal three-quarter-ounce pours: apple brandy, elderflower liqueur, orange liqueur, lemon. Nothing leads. The elderflower is floral honey against the orchard, and the orange liqueur is peel; the lemon is the whole sour. Coupe, apple garnish. It drinks as a Sidecar that split the cognac and the orange liqueur and put apple and elderflower in their place.
cocktails.history: A drink called Southern Point does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. Equal-parts sours of this shape are modern, and the elderflower half of it cannot predate Robert Cooper's St-Germain, launched in 2007. The nearest parent is the Sidecar: brandy, orange liqueur, and lemon. This card swaps cognac for apple brandy, splits the sweet between elderflower and orange liqueur, and pours all four at three-quarters of an ounce, shaken, in a coupe with an apple garnish.

refs.title: VinePair, 8 Things You Should Know About St-Germain Elderflower Liqueur

cocktails.name: Sidecar
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of cognac, a full ounce of orange liqueur, three-quarters lemon. The orange liqueur is heavier than the lemon, so the drink is peel and candy. Shaken, coupe, sugar rim.
cocktails.history: Robert Vermeire prints the Sidecar in May 1922 in Cocktails How to Mix Them: equal cognac, Cointreau, and lemon, very popular in France, and first introduced in London by Pat MacGarry of Buck's Club. Harry MacElhone, who had worked with MacGarry, prints the same formula later that year and later takes the credit himself. Frank Meier at the Ritz Bar in Paris listed it among cocktails new since the war. David Embury, in 1948, credits an unnamed American captain in a Paris sidecar. The origin stays disputed. This card pours an ounce and a half of cognac, a full ounce of orange liqueur, and three-quarters lemon, shaken, with a sugar rim.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Sidecar

cocktails.name: Buster Brown
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of demerara, three dashes of orange bitters. The lemon is a full sour; orange bitters are peel over the brown sugar. Shaken, coupe, orange twist.
cocktails.history: The Buster Brown prints in the 1933 Mixer's Guide as a whiskey cocktail: a teaspoon of gum, two dashes of lemon, two dashes of orange bitters, and a jigger of whisky, stirred and strained. The comic-strip boy of the same name had been running in American newspapers since 1902. This card turns those lemon dashes into three-quarters of an ounce, sweetens with half an ounce of demerara, shakes it, and keeps three dashes of orange bitters. Coupe, orange twist.

cocktails.name: Gold Rush
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, three-quarters honey syrup. Honey is thick and floral against the lemon. Shaken, rocks with ice. Bourbon, citrus, and a brown pour that sits.
cocktails.history: T.J. Siegal, a childhood friend of Sasha Petraske, asked for honey syrup in his bourbon sour at Milk & Honey in New York around 2000, shortly after Petraske opened the bar on New Year's Eve 1999. Siegal named it while drinking the first one. Robert Simonson traces the story in Punch; Sam Ross later built the Penicillin from the same honey-sour idea. This card keeps the two ounces of bourbon and three-quarters each of lemon and honey syrup, over ice. No twist.

refs.title: Punch, How the Gold Rush Became a Modern Classic

cocktails.name: Whiskey Sour
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of demerara, egg white. The foam is the texture; demerara is brown sugar under the lemon. Shaken, rocks with ice, cherry and lemon. A short sour with a dry cap.
cocktails.history: A whisky sour is named as early as 1826, and Jerry Thomas prints sours in 1862. The Waukesha Plain Dealer uses the name in 1870 without explaining it. Paul Clarke, in The Oxford Companion, tracks egg white as a European addition from the 1920s that was common in America by the 1940s. The Atlanta Daily Constitution put it in 1879: when American meets American, then comes the whisky sour. This card pours two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of demerara, egg white, over ice with cherry and lemon. No wine float.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Whisky Sour

cocktails.name: Expat
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, a full ounce of lime, half an ounce of simple, two dashes of Angostura. Lime, so the sour is sharp and green; the sugar is thin against that ounce of juice. Shaken, coupe, mint. Clove on the lime.
cocktails.history: Lauren Schell built the Expat at Little Branch in Manhattan in 2009. She did not name it until she moved overseas and the bar kept sending the bourbon shake out; Expat seemed the obvious word. Erick Castro printed the spec in Eater in 2015: two ounces of bourbon, an ounce of lime, three-quarters simple, Angostura, mint. This card keeps the bourbon, the full ounce of lime, the mint, and the dashes, yet it pours only half an ounce of simple.

refs.title: Eater, Nine Awesome Cocktails That Should Be Considered Modern Classics

cocktails.name: Whiskey Daisy
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters lemon, a quarter of orange liqueur, one barspoon of simple. The orange liqueur is peel in the sugar slot. Shaken, rocks with ice. A short sour that sits.
cocktails.history: Jerry Thomas prints the Daisy in the 1876 Bar-Tender's Guide as a sour sweetened with orange liqueur and topped with seltzer, in brandy, whiskey, gin, and rum versions. David Wondrich, in The Oxford Companion, notes an 1883 claim that Billy Taylor gave the idea to Frank Haas at Fred Eberlin's bar near the New York Stock Exchange about 1873. Later daisies swapped grenadine for curaçao and went long. This card keeps the whiskey, lemon, and orange liqueur, adds a barspoon of simple, and pours it over ice with no soda.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Daisy

cocktails.name: Man o' War
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters orange liqueur, half an ounce each of sweet vermouth and lemon. The orange liqueur is heavier than the lemon, so peel leads. Shaken, coupe, lemon twist. A Manhattan sour: grape, whiskey, and candy citrus.
cocktails.history: The drink is named for the thoroughbred who won 20 of 21 races in 1919 and 1920, including the Preakness and Belmont. Simon Difford finds no mid-century book recipe and treats the cocktail as modern; a 1915 newspaper Man-o'-war cocktail is condensed milk, alcohol, and eggs. The Indianapolis Star printed the bourbon, Cointreau, sweet vermouth, and lemon formula in 2015 as a Derby drink. This card pours two ounces of bourbon, three-quarters orange liqueur, half each of sweet vermouth and lemon, coupe, lemon twist.

cocktails.name: Little Honey
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of bourbon, three-quarters elderflower, half an ounce each of dry vermouth and lemon, a quarter of honey, egg white. The foam carries the flower; dry vermouth keeps it lean. Shaken, rocks with ice, orange twist. Bourbon under elderflower.
cocktails.history: A drink called Little Honey does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The nearest parents are the Gold Rush, T.J. Siegal's bourbon, lemon, and honey sour at Milk & Honey around 2000, and the Bee's Knees, with St-Germain, launched by Robert Cooper in 2007, in the elderflower slot. This card adds dry vermouth and egg white, pours an ounce and a half of bourbon, and serves it over ice with an orange twist.

refs.title: Punch, How the Gold Rush Became a Modern Classic
VinePair, 8 Things You Should Know About St-Germain Elderflower Liqueur

cocktails.name: Lemon Drop
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of vodka, three-quarters orange liqueur, a full ounce of lemon, one barspoon of simple. The lemon is louder than the orange liqueur; a barspoon of sugar barely covers an ounce of juice. Shaken, coupe, sugar rim. Candy, then pith.
cocktails.history: Norman Hobday, who ran Henry Africa's in San Francisco, the fern bar that opened in 1969, built the Lemon Drop in the 1970s as a vodka sour in a sugar-rimmed cocktail glass. Martin Cate, in The Oxford Companion, files it with the Harvey Wallbanger and the wine spritzer. Later bars reduced it to a chilled vodka shot with a sugared lemon wedge. This card keeps the glass and the sugar rim, with two ounces of vodka, three-quarters orange liqueur, a full ounce of lemon, and a barspoon of simple.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Lemon Drop

cocktails.name: Katinka
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of vodka, three-quarters apricot liqueur, half an ounce of lime. Stone fruit and lime; the apricot sweetens the sour by itself. Shaken, coupe. Short, tart apricot.
cocktails.history: David Embury prints a Katinka in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks (1948): vodka, apricot liqueur, and lime. Haus Alpenz reprints that spec as two ounces of vodka and half an ounce each of apricot and lime. This card is leaner on the vodka and heavier on the apricot: an ounce and a half, three-quarters, and half a lime, shaken, coupe.

cocktails.name: Queen Bee
cocktails.taste: Three-quarters each of vodka, elderflower, and lemon, a quarter of honey, an ounce of Champagne. The Champagne is the volume. Shaken, then the wine, coupe, lemon twist. Flower, honey, bubbles, a small drink that foams from the fizz.
cocktails.history: Charles H. Baker prints a Queen Bee in 1951 The South American Gentleman's Companion on apple brandy, lemon, honey, and curaçao; that is not this drink. A vodka, elderflower, lemon, honey, and Champagne Queen Bee does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals. St-Germain, the elderflower liqueur this card calls for, launched in 2007. This card pours three-quarters each of vodka, elderflower, and lemon, a quarter of honey syrup, and an ounce of Champagne, coupe, lemon twist.

refs.title: Punch, Bring Back the Queen Bee
VinePair, 8 Things You Should Know About St-Germain Elderflower Liqueur

cocktails.name: Gimlet
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin against three-quarters of lime, so the lime is loud, then a half ounce of simple. Shaken, coupe. The lime is fresh and tart; the syrup is a thin coat of sugar, enough to take the edge. Juniper under citrus.
cocktails.history: Lauchlan Rose of Edinburgh patented an alcohol-free lime cordial in 1867, the same year the Merchant Shipping Act required British ships to carry lime juice against scurvy. Officers mixing gin with Rose's is the navy story; a gimlet is also a barrel tap. The first named print is Harry MacElhone's 1922 Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails: equal parts Plymouth gin and Rose's, "a very popular beverage in the Navy." Rear-Admiral Sir Thomas Desmond Gimlette is sometimes credited; his Times obituary does not mention the drink. This card pours two ounces of gin, three-quarters of fresh lime, and a half ounce of simple, coupe.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, A Gimlet

cocktails.name: French 75
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin against a full ounce of lemon, so the citrus is a real pour, then a half ounce of simple and three ounces of Champagne. Shaken, then the wine. Rocks with ice and a lemon twist, not a flute. The lemon stays loud over the bubbles; the cube melts into it.
cocktails.history: The name is the French 75-millimetre field gun of the First World War. The first drink so called, reported by O. O. McIntyre in the Washington Herald in 1915, is gin, applejack, grenadine, and lemon; Robert Vermeire, in 1922, credits Henry Tépé of Henry's Bar in Paris. The gin, lemon, sugar, and Champagne formula first prints in Judge Jr's 1927 Here's How, in a tall glass: if you use club soda, you have a Tom Collins. Harry Craddock repeats it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, poured over cracked ice. The flute is later. This card keeps the gin and the ice, yet it pours a full ounce of lemon and three of Champagne into a rocks glass with a lemon twist.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The French 75

cocktails.name: Bennett
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of lime, a half ounce of simple, two dashes of Angostura. The bitters are bark and clove under the lime. Shaken, coupe. Lime, juniper, and a bitter finish. A Gimlet with spice, not honey.
cocktails.history: Robert Vermeire prints the Bennett in 1922 Cocktails: How to Mix Them: two-sixths of a gill of Old Tom, one-sixth fresh lime, two dashes of Angostura, no sugar. "This cocktail, which is very popular in Chili, is called after the well-known and popular landowner and millionaire of that country." Nakata Seizo repeats it in Japan in 1926; Jimmy of Ciro's London does the same in 1930. The Chilean namesake is not further identified. This card adds a half ounce of simple, pours an ounce and a half of gin and three-quarters of lime, two dashes of Angostura, coupe.

cocktails.name: Gin Sour
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lemon, a half ounce of simple, and egg white. The white is foam and a silk coat; the lemon is tart underneath. Shaken, rocks with ice, lemon twist. It sits: gin, citrus, and a head that lasts while the cube melts.
cocktails.history: Jerry Thomas prints the Gin Sour in 1862 How to Mix Drinks as the Gin Fix without the fruit: sugar, water, lemon, gin, in a small bar glass. A sour is a punch for one. The first record of the name is an 1856 list at Mart Ackermann's Saloon in Toronto. Egg white is later; Eddie Clark's 1947 King Cocktail and the 1955 UKBG guide treat it as optional, not original. This card pours two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lemon, a half ounce of simple, and egg white, over ice with a lemon twist.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, History of sour cocktails

cocktails.name: Bee's Knees
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin, three-quarters of lemon, three-quarters of honey syrup, so the honey is a full partner to the citrus. Shaken, coupe. The honey is floral and thick where simple would be thin; the lemon keeps it tart. Gin, pith, and a coat of honey.
cocktails.history: The Bee's Knees first prints in 1929, twice. Cocktails de Paris credits Frank Meier, head bartender at the Hotel Ritz in Paris from 1921; Meier reprints it in his 1936 The Artistry of Mixing Drinks. A Brooklyn Standard Union piece of 23 April 1929, cited by Jared Brown and Anistatia Miller, ascribes the drink to Mrs. J.J. Brown of Denver and Paris, Margaret Brown of the Titanic. David Embury, in 1948, calls the equal-parts gin, lemon, and honey a pernicious Prohibition recipe meant to cover vile gin, and dries it out. Both claims stay in print. This card pours two ounces of gin and three-quarters each of lemon and honey syrup, coupe.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, Bee's Knees

cocktails.name: Pegu Club
cocktails.taste: One and three-quarters ounces of gin against three-quarters of orange liqueur and only a half ounce of lime, so the lime is a squeeze under the peel. One dash of Angostura and one of orange bitters sit on the orange, bark and pith over a small lime. Shaken, coupe. Gin, candied orange, and a thin lime line.
cocktails.history: The Pegu Club was the house cocktail of the British officers' club of the same name, just outside Rangoon, Burma, now Yangon. Who mixed the first one is unknown. Harry MacElhone prints it in the 1920s: gin, orange curacao, lime, and a dash each of Angostura and orange bitters. Harry Craddock reprints it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book as a drink that has travelled, and is asked for, round the world. Craddock's lime is a teaspoon of Rose's; Jimmy, late of Ciro's, equalizes the curacao and the lime that same year. This card pours one and three-quarters gin, three-quarters orange liqueur, half an ounce of lime, and one dash of each bitters.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Pegu Club Cocktail
The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Pegu Club Cocktail

cocktails.name: White Lady
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters each of orange liqueur and lemon, a barspoon of simple, and egg white. The white is foam and a silk coat over lemon pith and candied peel. The barspoon of simple is a thin sweetness against equal orange and lemon. Shaken, coupe.
cocktails.history: Two drinks share the name. Harry MacElhone prints a White Lady in 1922 in Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails as brandy, creme de menthe, and Cointreau. The gin, lemon, and Cointreau version prints in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book at half gin and a quarter each of Cointreau and lemon, with no egg. MacElhone later claimed a 1929 gin revision at Harry's New York Bar in Paris; Victor Cabrin at London's Grosvenor House also claimed 1929. Egg white is later, New York in the late 1930s. This card is gin, orange liqueur, lemon, a barspoon of simple, and egg white.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, White Lady
The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), White Lady Cocktail

cocktails.name: Fine and Dandy
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters orange liqueur, three-quarters lemon, a barspoon of simple. Two dashes of Angostura pull bark and clove through the orange. Shaken, coupe. Peel, pith, and a little clove on the gin.
cocktails.history: The Fine and Dandy prints in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book: a quarter lemon, a quarter Cointreau, half Plymouth gin, and one dash of Angostura, shaken. It is a White Lady with bitters and without egg, under another name. Craddock does not claim it. This card keeps the two-to-one gin against equal orange liqueur and lemon, adds a barspoon of simple, and doubles the bitters to two dashes.

refs.title: The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Fine and Dandy Cocktail

cocktails.name: Jasmine
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin against three-quarters of lemon; a quarter each of Campari and orange liqueur. The Campari is bitter orange in a sour, so the drink reads pink and like grapefruit. Shaken, coupe, lemon twist. Gin, pith, and a thin bitter film.
cocktails.history: Paul Harrington mixed the first Jasmine in 1993 at Townhouse Bar and Grill in Emeryville, California, for Matt Jasmin, a classmate who asked for something Harrington had never made. Harrington riffed on a Pegu Club he knew from Trader Vic's: Campari in place of the two bitters, lemon in place of lime, and a lemon twist. He misspelled Jasmin's name and the drink kept the extra e. It prints in Cocktail: The Drinks Bible for the 21st Century, which Harrington wrote with Laura Moorhead in 1998. This card is Harrington's pour: an ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters lemon, a quarter each of Campari and orange liqueur, coupe, lemon twist.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Jasmine

cocktails.name: Rendezvous
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin, half an ounce of maraschino, half an ounce of lime. The cherry liqueur is almond and pit as much as fruit, and it does all the sweetening. Equal maraschino and lime, so neither wins. Shaken, coupe. Gin, cherry stone, and a tart lime line.
cocktails.history: Diane Lapis and Anne Peck-Davis print a Rendezvous Cocktail in Cocktails Across America (2018), dated 1938 and tied to the Muehlebach Hotel in Kansas City: one ounce of gin, half an ounce of maraschino, half an ounce of lime. The hotel opened in 1915. A different modern drink of the same name is gin, Campari, and kirsch; that is not this pour. This card scales the 1938 hotel drink to an ounce and a half of gin against half an ounce each of maraschino and lime, shaken, coupe.

refs.title: Diane Lapis and Anne Peck-Davis, Cocktails Across America (2018)

cocktails.name: Pendennis Club
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of gin against a full ounce of apricot liqueur, so the stone fruit is a third of the drink. Three-quarters lime is tart against the apricot; two dashes of Peychaud's pull cherry and anise through it. Shaken, coupe, lemon twist and a wheel. Pink, lime, and apricot.
cocktails.history: The Pendennis Club in Louisville, founded in 1881, gives the drink its name. Two recipes print under it. William T. Boothby's 1908 World's Drinks lists gin, apricot brandy, and French vermouth, no lime. Charles H. Baker's 1939 Gentleman's Companion calls it The Pendennis Club's Famous Special: gin, dry apricot brandy, lime or lemon, two dashes of Peychaud's, strained over a split kumquat. The club later lost the running story of who mixed it. This card is Baker's sour: two ounces of gin, one of apricot, three-quarters lime, two dashes of Peychaud's, shaken, with a lemon twist and a wheel and no kumquat.

refs.title: Toby Cecchini, The Secret Signature Cocktail of Louisville, Saveur

cocktails.name: Hat Tip
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of gin, three-quarters elderflower, a quarter of Campari, half an ounce of lemon, a barspoon of simple. The elderflower is the sweet; Campari is a bitter pink film. Shaken, coupe. Floral gin, lemon pith, and a thin bitter edge.
