cocktails.history: No first printing or named bartender turned up for the Hat Tip. Elderflower liqueur in this form dates to St-Germain, launched in 2007, so the combination is recent. This card shakes an ounce and a half of gin with three-quarters elderflower, a quarter of Campari, half an ounce of lemon, and a barspoon of simple, in a coupe.

cocktails.name: Olivette
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of gin and dry vermouth, a fifty-fifty Martini, with a half ounce of elderflower as the sweet. No juice, no bitters. Shaken, so it clouds a little. Coupe, olive. Floral gin, dry wine, and a brine finish.
cocktails.history: Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book prints an Olivette Cocktail of Plymouth gin, absinthe, orange bitters, and syrup, with an olive; that is not this drink. This card's Olivette is gin, dry vermouth, and elderflower, the formula St-Germain publishes as a house cocktail: equal gin and Noilly Prat, half an ounce of the liqueur, green olive. St-Germain itself dates to 2007. Dante in New York bottles a related Olivette Martini with both vodka and gin. This card shakes the St-Germain pour and keeps the olive.

refs.title: The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), Olivette Cocktail

cocktails.name: Margarita
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of tequila against three-quarters each of orange liqueur and lime. The tequila is the drink; the orange and lime are equal and small, peel and acid around agave. Shaken, coupe, salt rim. Short, no ice in the glass.
cocktails.history: The origin is a pile of claims. William J. Tarling prints the same three ingredients as the Picador in the 1937 Cafe Royal Cocktail Book in London. Charlie Connolly's 1939 Cotton Club booklet has a Tequila Sour with Cointreau, lime, and a salt rim. Under the name Margarita it surfaces in a 1953 Santa Rosa Press Democrat item from Ensenada. Claimants include Danny Negrete at Tehuacan in 1936, Johnny Durlesser at the Tail o' the Cock in Los Angeles, Pancho Morales in Juarez in 1942, Danny Herrera at Rancho La Gloria, and Margaret Sames in Acapulco in 1948. This card pours two ounces of tequila, three-quarters orange liqueur, three-quarters lime, shaken, in a coupe with salt.

refs.title: The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails, The Margarita
Difford's Guide, History of the Margarita cocktail

cocktails.name: Mexican Firing Squad
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of tequila, three-quarters grenadine, three-quarters lime. Equal pomegranate and lime, a pink tequila sour. Two dashes of Angostura pull clove through the fruit. Shaken, coupe, cherry. Short.
cocktails.history: Charles H. Baker records the Mexican Firing Squad Special in The Gentleman's Companion, Volume II (1939), as a drink he found at La Cucaracha Bar in Mexico City in 1937: two jiggers tequila, juice of two small limes, one and a half to two teaspoons of grenadine, two dashes of Angostura, in a tall collins packed with cracked ice, garnished with orange, pineapple, and cherry. Period menus from the bar do not list it; it may have been off-menu. This card keeps the tequila, grenadine, lime, and Angostura, equalizes the grenadine and lime at three-quarters, and pours it short in a coupe with a cherry.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, Mexican Firing Squad Special

cocktails.name: Vermouth-arita
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of tequila against a full ounce of sweet vermouth, so the wine is a second base. Half an ounce of orange liqueur and half of lime are the Margarita's other two, cut down. Shaken, rocks, ice, cherry. A tequila Manhattan that took a lime.
cocktails.history: A drink called Vermouth-arita does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The parent is the Margarita: tequila, orange liqueur, and lime, a formula in print by 1937 as William J. Tarling's Picador and under this name by 1953. This card keeps the tequila and the shake, puts a full ounce of sweet vermouth in the glass, cuts the orange liqueur and lime to half an ounce each, and pours it over ice with a cherry.

refs.title: Difford's Guide, History of the Margarita cocktail

cocktails.name: Stingless Bee
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of tequila, three-quarters honey syrup, half lime, half lemon. The citrus is split, so neither fruit wins; the honey is waxier than sugar. Egg white gives it a foam cap. Three dashes of Peychaud's are dropped on the foam, cherry-anise on the white. Coupe.
cocktails.history: The Bee's Knees is a gin sour with honey, first printed in Paris around 1929. Frank Meier's Bar de Ritz recipe appears in Cocktails de Paris that year; a Brooklyn Standard Union article of 22 April 1929 credits Mrs. J.J. Brown of Denver and Paris, later called Molly Brown. Both claims stay in print. A drink called Stingless Bee does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals, nor under that name in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. This card swaps gin for tequila, splits the citrus between lime and lemon, shakes egg white, and drops three dashes of Peychaud's on the foam.

cocktails.name: Mickie Walker
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of scotch, then a half ounce each of sweet vermouth, grenadine, and lemon. The lemon and pomegranate are real pours, not dashes, so the drink is shaken and pink. Coupe, cherry. Scotch, grape, and a sour pomegranate cut.
cocktails.history: Harry Craddock prints the Mickie Walker Cocktail in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930: one dash grenadine, one dash lemon juice, a quarter Italian vermouth, three-quarters Scotch whisky, shaken. The spelling is Craddock's; the name tracks Edward Patrick "Mickey" Walker, the New Jersey boxer who took the welterweight title in 1922 and the middleweight in 1926. The 1937 UKBG Approved Cocktails repeats Craddock's dashes. This card keeps the name Mickie Walker and the four ingredients, yet it pours a half ounce each of vermouth, grenadine, and lemon against an ounce and a half of scotch.

cocktails.name: Scofflaw
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of rye and dry vermouth, so the wine is half the drink. Half an ounce of grenadine, half of lemon, one dash of orange bitters. Shaken, coupe, orange twist. The rye is spice, the grenadine pomegranate, the lemon a sour cut through the dry vermouth.
cocktails.history: Delcevare King, a Massachusetts teetotaler, ran a 1924 contest for a word to shame drinkers who flouted Prohibition; Henry Irving Shaw and Kate L. Butler split the prize for "scofflaw." The Chicago Tribune reported a Scofflaw cocktail at Maxim's in Paris on 21 January 1924: three parts rye, two parts French vermouth, a dash of lemon and of grenadine. Harry MacElhone claimed Jock at Harry's New York Bar invented it days later, with orange bitters and equal Canadian Club and French vermouth. Difford's notes the Tribune piece on Maxim's predates MacElhone's claim. This card is one to one rye to dry vermouth, half an ounce each of grenadine and lemon, one dash of orange bitters, shaken, coupe, orange.

cocktails.name: Harvest Sour
cocktails.taste: Equal ounces of rye and apple brandy. Three-quarters of an ounce of lemon, half an ounce of simple, egg white. The foam is the texture; grated cinnamon on the coupe is the spice. Orchard, pepper, lemon, and a dry foam.
cocktails.history: The Harvest Sour is Sam Ross at Attaboy in New York, printed by Punch and dated by Difford's to around 2017: one ounce rye, one ounce applejack, three-quarters lemon, three-quarters simple, egg white, apple slice and cinnamon. Ross's other split-base drinks, the Paper Plane among them, are the parent method. A drink of this name does not appear in the pre-1970 manuals. This card keeps the equal rye and apple brandy, the lemon, the egg white, and the cinnamon. It pours half an ounce of simple rather than three-quarters, and it skips the apple slice.

cocktails.name: Queen Elizabeth
cocktails.taste: An ounce and a half of dry vermouth, three-quarters of Bénédictine, three-quarters of lime. No base spirit. The liqueur is honey and herbs; the lime matches it, so the drink is tart as well as sweet. Shaken, coupe. Vermouth and Bénédictine, then pith.
cocktails.history: Queen Elizabeth is a crowded name. This card is the vermouth one: dry vermouth, Bénédictine, and lime, with no gin and no brandy. David Wondrich found the formula in a Bénédictine advertisement in the February 1935 Esquire, billed as the prize-winning recipe in a nationwide cocktail contest. Difford's Guide credits Herbert L. Quick, head bartender at the Benjamin Franklin Hotel in Philadelphia in 1934, who named it for his wife, not the monarch. Other Queen Elizabeths in the manuals are gin drinks, or brandy and sweet vermouth. This card pours an ounce and a half of dry vermouth and three-quarters each of Bénédictine and lime.

cocktails.name: Dry Vermouth Sour
cocktails.taste: Two ounces of dry vermouth, three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of simple, egg white. The foam is the texture; the vermouth is the spirit, so the sour is grape and lemon under a dry foam. Shaken, coupe. A short sour with a dry cap.
cocktails.history: A drink called Dry Vermouth Sour does not appear under that name in the pre-1970 manuals, nor in Difford's, Punch, or Imbibe. The parent is the sour itself: spirit, citrus, and sugar, printed by Jerry Thomas in 1862, with egg white common in American sours by the 1940s. Vermouth as a base is older still; J. Haney's 1869 Steward and Barkeeper's Manual already has a Vermuth Cocktail, and Harry Johnson's 1882 manual dresses vermouth with gum, bitters, and maraschino. This card puts two ounces of dry vermouth through the sour template: three-quarters lemon, half an ounce of simple, egg white, coupe.
